injections of morphine, a rat develops tolerance to it.","printedPage":464,"pdfPage":482,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":120},{"text":"Symptoms of alcohol withdrawal include irritability, fatigue, shaking, sweating, and nausea.","printedPage":464,"pdfPage":482,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":121},{"text":"Cocaine is addictive even though the withdrawal symptoms are mild.","printedPage":465,"pdfPage":483,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":122},{"text":"Gambling can be a powerful addiction, even though no substance is withdrawn.","printedPage":465,"pdfPage":483,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":123}],"originalFacts":9,"additionalFacts":4,"glossary":[{"term":"Withdrawal","definition":"effects of drug cessation","sourcePrintedPage":635,"sourcePdfPage":653},{"term":"Tolerance","definition":"decreased effect of a drug after repeated use","sourcePrintedPage":634,"sourcePdfPage":652},{"term":"Frequency","definition":"the number of cycles per second, measured in Hz","sourcePrintedPage":623,"sourcePdfPage":641}],"sourceBodyWordsAvailable":234,"sourceStatus":"source_explained","mdCrosscheck":"terms_present","wordCount":198},{"id":"bp14-m14-1-h05","title":"Drug Use for Stress Reduction","level":2,"parentId":"bp14-m14-1-h01","printedPage":465,"pdfPage":483,"facts":[{"text":"One reason for an addiction is that a user learns to use the substance (or gambling habit or other addiction) to cope with stress.","printedPage":465,"pdfPage":483,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":45},{"text":"Researchers gave rats an opportunity to press a lever to inject themselves with heroin.","printedPage":465,"pdfPage":483,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":46},{"text":"Midway through the withdrawal period, some of the rats had an opportunity to self-administer heroin again, while others went through withdrawal without heroin.","printedPage":465,"pdfPage":483,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":47},{"text":"Later, when rats went through withdrawal a second time, all the rats had an opportunity to press a lever to try to get heroin, but this time, the lever was inoperative.","printedPage":465,"pdfPage":483,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":48},{"text":"Evidently, receiving an addictive drug during a withdrawal period is a powerful experience.","printedPage":465,"pdfPage":483,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":49},{"text":"Although both groups of rats pressed the lever, those that had self-administered heroin during the previous withdrawal state pressed more frequently.","printedPage":465,"pdfPage":483,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":124},{"text":"Users—rat or human—learn that the drug relieves the distress caused by drug withdrawal.","printedPage":465,"pdfPage":483,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":125},{"text":"The users then crave the drug during other kinds of distress.","printedPage":465,"pdfPage":483,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":126}],"originalFacts":5,"additionalFacts":3,"glossary":[{"term":"Withdrawal","definition":"effects of drug cessation","sourcePrintedPage":635,"sourcePdfPage":653}],"sourceBodyWordsAvailable":159,"sourceStatus":"source_explained","mdCrosscheck":"terms_present","wordCount":150},{"id":"bp14-m14-1-h06","title":"Predispositions","level":1,"parentId":null,"printedPage":465,"pdfPage":483,"facts":[{"text":"Most people drink alcohol in moderation, but others develop a habit of abuse.","printedPage":465,"pdfPage":483,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":51},{"text":"Even among mice, some develop compulsive alcohol use when given the opportunity, and some do not .","printedPage":465,"pdfPage":483,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":52},{"text":"A great deal of the predisposition depends on experience.","printedPage":465,"pdfPage":483,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":53},{"text":"People who had abusive experiences in childhood are more vulnerable, as is a child whose mother drank too much alcohol during pregnancy .","printedPage":465,"pdfPage":483,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":54},{"text":"Children who grew up without careful parental supervision are more likely to develop impulse problems than children of more attentive parents .","printedPage":465,"pdfPage":483,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":55},{"text":"As a rule, people with early-onset alcoholism (before age 25) have a family history of alcoholism, a genetic predisposition, and a rapid onset of the problem.","printedPage":465,"pdfPage":483,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":56},{"text":"With other substances also, only some of the users develop an addiction.","printedPage":465,"pdfPage":483,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":127},{"text":"People with later onset are more likely to have reacted to life difficulties, less likely to have a family history of alcoholism, and more likely to respond well to treatment.","printedPage":465,"pdfPage":483,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":128}],"originalFacts":6,"additionalFacts":2,"glossary":[],"sourceBodyWordsAvailable":186,"sourceStatus":"source_explained","mdCrosscheck":"terms_present","wordCount":152},{"id":"bp14-m14-1-h07","title":"Genetic Influences","level":2,"parentId":"bp14-m14-1-h06","printedPage":465,"pdfPage":483,"facts":[{"text":"The probability of abusing alcohol or other drugs also relates to genetic influences.","printedPage":465,"pdfPage":483,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":58},{"text":"Parents’ alcohol use correlates more strongly with that of their biological children than their adopted children .","printedPage":465,"pdfPage":483,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":59},{"text":"Several genes affect the probability of substance use, with effects that vary from one environment to another .","printedPage":465,"pdfPage":483,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":60},{"text":"Most of these genes are non-specific, increasing the risk of several mental disorders, and risk-taking behaviors in general .","printedPage":465,"pdfPage":483,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":61},{"text":"One gene with a well-confirmed influence on alcohol abuse controls the metabolism of alcohol.","printedPage":465,"pdfPage":483,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":62},{"text":"In fact, this is the only case of a common gene with a substantial effect on a human psychological disorder (other than Huntington’s disease).","printedPage":465,"pdfPage":483,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":63},{"text":"People with a gene that produces less acetaldehyde dehydrogenase metabolize acetaldehyde more slowly.","printedPage":465,"pdfPage":483,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":64},{"text":"If they drink much alcohol, they accumulate acetaldehyde, which produces flushing of the face, increased heart rate, nausea, headache, abdominal pain, impaired breathing, and tissue damage.","printedPage":465,"pdfPage":483,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":65},{"text":"After anyone drinks ethyl alcohol, enzymes in the liver metabolize it to acetaldehyde, a toxic substance.","printedPage":465,"pdfPage":483,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":129},{"text":"More than a third of the people in China and Japan have a gene that slows acetaldehyde metabolism.","printedPage":465,"pdfPage":483,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":130},{"text":"Probably for that reason, alcohol abuse has historically been uncommon in those countries.","printedPage":465,"pdfPage":483,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":131}],"originalFacts":8,"additionalFacts":3,"glossary":[{"term":"Huntington’s disease","definition":"neurological disorder characterized by jerky arm movements and facial twitches and later by tremors, writhing movements, and psychological symptoms","sourcePrintedPage":625,"sourcePdfPage":643}],"sourceBodyWordsAvailable":248,"sourceStatus":"source_explained","mdCrosscheck":"terms_present","wordCount":191},{"id":"bp14-m14-1-h08","title":"Behavioral Predictors of Abuse","level":2,"parentId":"bp14-m14-1-h06","printedPage":466,"pdfPage":484,"facts":[{"text":"If genes, early environment, or anything else predisposes certain people to drug or alcohol abuse, presumably the predisposition alters behavioral reactions to the substance.","printedPage":466,"pdfPage":484,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":67},{"text":"By the time someone has developed a serious substance abuse problem, overcoming it is difficult.","printedPage":466,"pdfPage":484,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":68},{"text":"Such studies find that alcoholism is more likely among those who were described in childhood as impulsive, risk taking, easily bored, sensation seeking, and outgoing .","printedPage":466,"pdfPage":484,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":69},{"text":"Because of the strong familial tendency toward alcoholism, researchers expect that many of the sons of alcoholics are future alcoholics themselves.","printedPage":466,"pdfPage":484,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":70},{"text":"The most robust finding is that most sons of alcoholics show less than average intoxication after drinking a moderate amount of alcohol.","printedPage":466,"pdfPage":484,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":71},{"text":"Presumably, someone who starts feeling tipsy after a couple of drinks stops at that point.","printedPage":466,"pdfPage":484,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":72},{"text":"Follow-up studies found that men who report low intoxication after moderate drinking are more likely than others to develop an alcohol abuse problem .","printedPage":466,"pdfPage":484,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":73},{"text":"If so, it should be possible to monitor behavior of young people and predict their risk for later problems.","printedPage":466,"pdfPage":484,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":132},{"text":"Other research follows this design: First, identify young men who are not yet problem drinkers.","printedPage":466,"pdfPage":484,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":133},{"text":"If someone with strong intoxication from a moderate intake does develop an alcohol problem, it is usually less severe than that of other abusers.","printedPage":466,"pdfPage":484,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":134},{"text":"The advice is, if you “hold your liquor well,” it is not something to brag about, but something to worry about.","printedPage":466,"pdfPage":484,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":135}],"originalFacts":7,"additionalFacts":4,"glossary":[],"sourceBodyWordsAvailable":411,"sourceStatus":"source_explained","mdCrosscheck":"terms_present","wordCount":226},{"id":"bp14-m14-1-h09","title":"Treatments","level":1,"parentId":null,"printedPage":466,"pdfPage":484,"facts":[{"text":"Research has revealed much about the mechanisms of addiction.","printedPage":466,"pdfPage":484,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":75},{"text":"Unfortunately, our increased understanding has not yet translated into better forms of treatment .","printedPage":466,"pdfPage":484,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":76},{"text":"In fact, that is the case for psychopathology in general.","printedPage":466,"pdfPage":484,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":77},{"text":"Research over recent decades has learned much about the genes, neurotransmitters, and other biological","printedPage":466,"pdfPage":484,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":78},{"text":"factors related to disorders, but treatment outcomes have not improved noticeably .","printedPage":467,"pdfPage":485,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":79},{"text":"The most common treatment for substance abuse, especially in the United States, is participation in Alcoholics Anonymous, Narcotics Anonymous, or similar organizations.","printedPage":467,"pdfPage":485,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":80},{"text":"A smaller number of people consult a psychotherapist.","printedPage":467,"pdfPage":485,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":81},{"text":"Not many people turn to medications, but a few options are available.","printedPage":467,"pdfPage":485,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":82}],"originalFacts":8,"additionalFacts":0,"glossary":[{"term":"Neurotransmitters","definition":"chemicals released by neurons that affect other neurons agonists and antagonists","sourcePrintedPage":628,"sourcePdfPage":646}],"sourceBodyWordsAvailable":105,"sourceStatus":"source_explained","mdCrosscheck":"terms_present","wordCount":101},{"id":"bp14-m14-1-h10","title":"Medications to Combat Alcohol Abuse","level":2,"parentId":"bp14-m14-1-h09","printedPage":467,"pdfPage":485,"facts":[{"text":"As mentioned, the liver metabolizes alcohol into acetaldehyde (toxic) and then into acetic acid (harmless).","printedPage":467,"pdfPage":485,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":84},{"text":"The drug disulfiram, which goes by the trade name Antabuse , antagonizes the enzyme that metabolizes acetaldehyde.","printedPage":467,"pdfPage":485,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":85},{"text":"Ordinarily, that result would indicate that a drug is ineffective, but Antabuse is a special case because of why it is similar to the placebo.","printedPage":467,"pdfPage":485,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":86},{"text":"Antabuse is about equal to placebo not because Antabuse is ineffective, but because thinking that a placebo might be Antabuse makes the placebo effective .","printedPage":467,"pdfPage":485,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":87},{"text":"A related idea is to have people drink alcohol and then immediately take a drug that produces nausea, thereby forming a learned aversion to the taste of the alcohol.","printedPage":467,"pdfPage":485,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":88},{"text":"That procedure usually produces quick and effective avoidance of alcohol, although its use has never been popular .","printedPage":467,"pdfPage":485,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":89},{"text":"Other medications are naloxone (trade name Revia) and naltrexone, which block opiate receptors and thereby decrease the pleasure from alcohol.","printedPage":467,"pdfPage":485,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":90},{"text":"Soon therapists tried using disulfiram as a drug, hoping that those with alcoholism would associate alcohol with illness and stop drinking.","printedPage":467,"pdfPage":485,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":136},{"text":"When people take Antabuse, or a placebo that they think might be Antabuse, the threat of becoming ill strongly discourages any attempt to drink alcohol.","printedPage":467,"pdfPage":485,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":137}],"originalFacts":7,"additionalFacts":2,"glossary":[{"term":"Antabuse","definition":"drug that antagonizes the effects of acetaldehyde dehydrogenase by binding to its copper ion","sourcePrintedPage":618,"sourcePdfPage":636}],"sourceBodyWordsAvailable":339,"sourceStatus":"source_explained","mdCrosscheck":"terms_present","wordCount":195},{"id":"bp14-m14-1-h11","title":"Medications to Combat Opiate Abuse","level":2,"parentId":"bp14-m14-1-h09","printedPage":467,"pdfPage":485,"facts":[{"text":"Some physicians at the time recommended that people using alcohol switch to heroin .","printedPage":467,"pdfPage":485,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":92},{"text":"Still, the idea has persisted that people who cannot quit opiates might switch to a less harmful drug.","printedPage":467,"pdfPage":485,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":93},{"text":"Methadone (METH-uh-don), similar to heroin and morphine, activates the same brain receptors and produces the same effects, but it has the advantage that it can be taken orally.","printedPage":467,"pdfPage":485,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":94},{"text":"Methadone taken orally slowly enters the blood and then the brain, avoiding a “rush” that disrupts behavior.","printedPage":467,"pdfPage":485,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":95},{"text":"Because methadone leaves the brain slowly, the withdrawal symptoms are also gradual.","printedPage":467,"pdfPage":485,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":96},{"text":"Buprenorphine and levomethadyl acetate (LAAM), drugs similar to methadone, are also used to treat opiate addiction.","printedPage":467,"pdfPage":485,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":97},{"text":"Anecdotal reports have stated that a drug called ibogaine reduces cravings and decreases the probability of drug relapse.","printedPage":467,"pdfPage":485,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":98},{"text":"However, ibogaine causes hallucinations, and it can damage the heart.","printedPage":467,"pdfPage":485,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":99},{"text":"So far, we know that it reduces alcohol and heroin seeking in mice, and we await results from human trials .","printedPage":467,"pdfPage":485,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":100},{"text":"Heroin is an artificial substance invented in the 1800s as a supposedly safer alternative for people who were trying to quit morphine.","printedPage":467,"pdfPage":485,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":138},{"text":"LAAM has the advantage of producing a longlasting effect so that the person visits a clinic three times a week instead of daily.","printedPage":467,"pdfPage":485,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":139}],"originalFacts":9,"additionalFacts":2,"glossary":[{"term":"Withdrawal","definition":"effects Closing: The Psychology and Biology of Substance Abuse","level":1,"parentId":null,"printedPage":468,"pdfPage":486,"facts":[{"text":"Many people say that alcoholism or other drug addiction is a disease.","printedPage":468,"pdfPage":486,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":102},{"text":"Dis-ease is literally lack of ease, so in a sense anything that causes difficulty in life is a disease.","printedPage":468,"pdfPage":486,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":103},{"text":"However, the term disease is generally taken to imply that the problem calls for medical intervention.","printedPage":468,"pdfPage":486,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":104},{"text":"Addiction alters the brain’s reaction to the drug, cues for the drug, and other events.","printedPage":468,"pdfPage":486,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":105},{"text":"Addiction is a complex problem that requires attention to both the physiology and the social environment.","printedPage":468,"pdfPage":486,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":106},{"text":"They’re also presented in alphabetical order with definitions in the book’s Subject Index/Glossary at the end of this book.","printedPage":468,"pdfPage":486,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":107},{"text":"The research on sensitization of the nucleus accumbens dealt with addictive drugs, mainly cocaine.","printedPage":468,"pdfPage":486,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":108},{"text":"Calling addiction a disease helps to reduce some of the guilt and stigma.","printedPage":468,"pdfPage":486,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":140},{"text":"As you have seen in this module, addiction does have a physiological basis.","printedPage":468,"pdfPage":486,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":141}],"originalFacts":7,"additionalFacts":2,"glossary":[{"term":"Nucleus Effects","level":1,"parentId":null,"printedPage":462,"pdfPage":480,"explanation":"Substance use affects the brain through several interacting processes: immediate drug action, learning from reward, adaptation with repeated exposure and life circumstances that promote continued use. No single process explains every substance or person.","paragraphIndex":20000,"bullets":[{"label":"Drug action","explanation":"Different substances influence receptors and transmitters in different ways, producing different effects on arousal, mood and behavior.","paragraphIndex":20001},{"label":"Diagnostic caution","explanation":"Repeated use alone is not identical to a use disorder; impairment, loss of control and harmful consequences are central to the clinical concern.","paragraphIndex":20002},{"label":"Direct and indirect effects","explanation":"Some substances mimic or block transmitter actions; others change release, reuptake, or the responsiveness of neural systems.","paragraphIndex":78100},{"label":"Important distinction","explanation":"Acute drug effects are not identical to the processes that lead to repeated use, compulsive use, tolerance, or withdrawal.","paragraphIndex":78101}],"status":"original_classroom_note_sample","basis":"provided_book_pdf_and_markdown","followUpExplanation":"Drugs can alter perception, mood, arousal, and behavior by interacting with receptors, transporters, and other parts of nervous-system chemistry. The effect varies with dose, situation, and the person's history.","followUpParagraphIndex":45400,"depth":"comprehensive_masters_with_expanded_explanations"},{"headingId":"bp14-m14-1-h02","title":"The Role of Dopamine","level":2,"parentId":"bp14-m14-1-h01","printedPage":463,"pdfPage":481,"explanation":"Dopamine signaling contributes to learning about rewards and the cues that predict them. The textbook cautions against calling dopamine simply the pleasure chemical.","paragraphIndex":20003,"bullets":[{"label":"Reinforcement","explanation":"Drug-associated dopamine changes can make behaviors and contexts more likely to attract attention and be repeated.","paragraphIndex":20004},{"label":"Predictive cues","explanation":"Environmental signals linked to drug use can acquire motivational power even when the drug's immediate pleasant effect weakens.","paragraphIndex":20005},{"label":"Reward prediction","explanation":"Drug effects can strongly influence the signals that teach an organism which actions and environments have important consequences.","paragraphIndex":78102},{"label":"Why this matters","explanation":"A person may continue seeking a drug even when the immediate experience is no longer especially pleasurable. Learned motivation and habits can persist after subjective enjoyment declines.","paragraphIndex":78103}],"status":"original_classroom_note_sample","basis":"provided_book_pdf_and_markdown","followUpExplanation":"Dopamine-related circuits contribute to learning about rewards and cues that predict them. Their importance to addiction is broader than the idea that dopamine simply produces pleasure.","followUpParagraphIndex":45401,"depth":"comprehensive_masters_with_expanded_explanations"},{"headingId":"bp14-m14-1-h03","title":"Cravings","level":2,"parentId":"bp14-m14-1-h01","printedPage":464,"pdfPage":482,"explanation":"Craving is a strong motivational state that can be triggered by bodily need, emotional distress or reminders of past drug taking. It helps explain relapse after abstinence.","paragraphIndex":20006,"bullets":[{"label":"Learned associations","explanation":"Places, people and moods present during drug use may later evoke a desire to use, even when the person consciously wants to stop.","paragraphIndex":20007},{"label":"Persistence","explanation":"An intense urge need not indicate that pleasure remains high; wanting and liking can diverge as the nervous system adapts.","paragraphIndex":20008},{"label":"Conditioned cues","explanation":"Places, people, emotions, or routines previously linked with use can acquire motivational power.","paragraphIndex":78104},{"label":"Relapse vulnerability","explanation":"The influence of such cues can remain after a period without the drug. Understanding craving helps explain why avoiding use once does not make future use effortless.","paragraphIndex":78105}],"status":"original_classroom_note_sample","basis":"provided_book_pdf_and_markdown","followUpExplanation":"Craving is a strong motivation to obtain a substance, often triggered by cues associated with earlier use. It is not just a conscious decision made after weighing costs and benefits.","followUpParagraphIndex":45402,"depth":"comprehensive_masters_with_expanded_explanations"},{"headingId":"bp14-m14-1-h04","title":"Tolerance and Withdrawal","level":2,"parentId":"bp14-m14-1-h01","printedPage":464,"pdfPage":482,"explanation":"Tolerance and withdrawal are related but distinct consequences of repeated exposure. Both involve adjustment to an altered physiological state.","paragraphIndex":20009,"bullets":[{"label":"Tolerance","explanation":"The same dose has a reduced effect over time, or a higher dose is needed to produce a similar effect; the mechanisms differ among drugs.","paragraphIndex":20010},{"label":"Withdrawal","explanation":"When regular use stops, opposing physiological adaptations can produce discomfort or disruption. Dependence, tolerance and a substance use disorder should not be treated as exact synonyms.","paragraphIndex":20011},{"label":"Tolerance","explanation":"After repeated exposure, the same dose may have less effect, or a larger amount may be required to obtain a familiar effect. Adaptation can differ across particular drug effects.","paragraphIndex":78106},{"label":"Withdrawal","explanation":"When adapted systems no longer receive the substance, uncomfortable or harmful reactions may emerge. Avoidance of withdrawal can become an additional reason for continued use.","paragraphIndex":78107}],"status":"original_classroom_note_sample","basis":"provided_book_pdf_and_markdown","followUpExplanation":"Tolerance and withdrawal are consequences of repeated exposure, although they do not perfectly predict whether a person will develop addiction.","followUpParagraphIndex":45403,"depth":"comprehensive_masters_with_expanded_explanations"},{"headingId":"bp14-m14-1-h05","title":"Drug Use for Stress Reduction","level":2,"parentId":"bp14-m14-1-h01","printedPage":465,"pdfPage":483,"explanation":"People may initially use a substance to dampen anxiety or stress, creating a powerful cycle when the relief is temporary.","paragraphIndex":20012,"bullets":[{"label":"Negative reinforcement","explanation":"If using a drug removes an unpleasant state, that relief can reinforce repeated use even without strong pleasure.","paragraphIndex":20013},{"label":"Long-term problem","explanation":"As adaptation and stress accumulate, the same substance may become part of the source of distress it was used to reduce.","paragraphIndex":20014},{"label":"Negative reinforcement","explanation":"If using a drug reduces a distressing state, that relief can increase the chance of using it again in similar circumstances.","paragraphIndex":78108},{"label":"Cycle of dependence","explanation":"Stress and withdrawal-related distress can become triggers for renewed use. Treatment must consider the person's environment as well as the pharmacology of the substance.","paragraphIndex":78109}],"status":"original_classroom_note_sample","basis":"provided_book_pdf_and_markdown","followUpExplanation":"Substance use may become a learned attempt to manage stress or negative emotion. Short-term relief can strengthen a behavior that creates longer-term difficulties.","followUpParagraphIndex":45404,"depth":"comprehensive_masters_with_expanded_explanations"},{"headingId":"bp14-m14-1-h06","title":"Predispositions","level":1,"parentId":null,"printedPage":465,"pdfPage":483,"explanation":"Risk of problematic substance use reflects a mixture of personal and environmental influences. A predisposition increases probability; it does not make the outcome inevitable.","paragraphIndex":20015,"bullets":[{"label":"Multiple pathways","explanation":"Impulsivity, stress exposure, access to substances, learning history and vulnerability to reward cues can combine in different ways.","paragraphIndex":20016},{"label":"Protective influences","explanation":"Changes in circumstance, support and behavior can alter a person's trajectory even when some underlying risks remain.","paragraphIndex":20017},{"label":"Multiple influences","explanation":"Family history, early life, patterns of impulsive behavior, and availability of substances may change the probability of problematic use.","paragraphIndex":78110},{"label":"Avoid determinism","explanation":"A predisposition is not a prediction for one individual. Social setting, opportunities, and protective factors also matter.","paragraphIndex":78111}],"status":"original_classroom_note_sample","basis":"provided_book_pdf_and_markdown","followUpExplanation":"Not everyone exposed to an addictive substance follows the same trajectory. Vulnerability reflects interacting personal characteristics, circumstances, and experiences.","followUpParagraphIndex":45405,"depth":"comprehensive_masters_with_expanded_explanations"},{"headingId":"bp14-m14-1-h07","title":"Genetic Influences","level":2,"parentId":"bp14-m14-1-h06","printedPage":465,"pdfPage":483,"explanation":"Genetic studies find inherited contributions to vulnerability, but no single gene determines substance abuse. Genes can influence both the response to drugs and traits related to repeated use.","paragraphIndex":20018,"bullets":[{"label":"Indirect effects","explanation":"Inherited variation may affect metabolism, subjective drug effects, impulsivity or susceptibility to stress.","paragraphIndex":20019},{"label":"Interpretation","explanation":"A family resemblance can reflect shared genes and shared environment; useful studies attempt to separate these contributions.","paragraphIndex":20020},{"label":"Heritability evidence","explanation":"Resemblance between biological relatives can exceed resemblance between people raised together without genetic relationship for some patterns of substance use.","paragraphIndex":78112},{"label":"Gene–environment interaction","explanation":"A genetic influence can affect broad traits such as risk taking, and its effects depend on the environment. There is no one gene that determines addiction.","paragraphIndex":78113}],"status":"original_classroom_note_sample","basis":"provided_book_pdf_and_markdown","followUpExplanation":"Studies of families, twins, and adopted children support genetic contributions to differences in substance-use risk, but the effect is spread across many factors.","followUpParagraphIndex":45406,"depth":"comprehensive_masters_with_expanded_explanations"},{"headingId":"bp14-m14-1-h08","title":"Behavioral Predictors of Abuse","level":2,"parentId":"bp14-m14-1-h06","printedPage":466,"pdfPage":484,"explanation":"Behavioral tendencies can predict risk without explaining it completely. Researchers examine traits that appear before heavy substance use to avoid mistaking consequences for causes.","paragraphIndex":20021,"bullets":[{"label":"Individual differences","explanation":"Novelty seeking, response to reward or difficulty inhibiting behavior may make particular patterns of use more likely.","paragraphIndex":20022},{"label":"Avoid overprediction","explanation":"Many people with a risk factor never develop problematic use, while others develop it without obvious early markers.","paragraphIndex":20023},{"label":"Behavioral prediction","explanation":"Researchers examine how traits measured before substantial use relate to later outcomes.","paragraphIndex":78114},{"label":"Interpretation","explanation":"A predictor is not necessarily a direct cause. Multiple pathways can lead to the same outcome, so a person's behavior should not be treated as an irreversible destiny.","paragraphIndex":78115}],"status":"original_classroom_note_sample","basis":"provided_book_pdf_and_markdown","followUpExplanation":"Certain early behavioral patterns predict elevated risk of later substance problems, but prediction is probabilistic. Risk-taking and difficulties regulating behavior are examples of relevant characteristics.","followUpParagraphIndex":45407,"depth":"comprehensive_masters_with_expanded_explanations"},{"headingId":"bp14-m14-1-h09","title":"Treatments","level":1,"parentId":null,"printedPage":466,"pdfPage":484,"explanation":"Effective treatment addresses more than acute chemical effects. Recovery may require changing learned cues, managing withdrawal, improving coping and altering the environment that sustains use.","paragraphIndex":20024,"bullets":[{"label":"Behavioral work","explanation":"Identifying high-risk situations, creating alternative responses and building ongoing support can reduce opportunities for relapse.","paragraphIndex":20025},{"label":"Medical contribution","explanation":"Some medications change rewarding drug effects, block receptors or reduce physiological symptoms, but their usefulness depends on the substance and person.","paragraphIndex":20026},{"label":"Behavioral support","explanation":"Approaches may work on coping skills, triggers, reinforcement, and maintaining changes in daily routines.","paragraphIndex":78116},{"label":"Medication and support","explanation":"For some substances, medication can reduce particular risks or symptoms; successful care also depends on follow-up and the individual's circumstances. These notes describe the textbook, not personal treatment advice.","paragraphIndex":78117}],"status":"original_classroom_note_sample","basis":"provided_book_pdf_and_markdown","followUpExplanation":"Treatment addresses biological adaptation, learned habits, stress, and the person's social context. There is no single intervention that is right for every substance or every individual.","followUpParagraphIndex":45408,"depth":"comprehensive_masters_with_expanded_explanations"},{"headingId":"bp14-m14-1-h10","title":"Medications to Combat Alcohol Abuse","level":2,"parentId":"bp14-m14-1-h09","printedPage":467,"pdfPage":485,"explanation":"Alcohol-use treatments may work by changing the body's response to alcohol or modifying systems that participate in reward. Medication is one component rather than a substitute for support.","paragraphIndex":20027,"bullets":[{"label":"Different targets","explanation":"Some approaches make drinking aversive; others reduce the reinforcement or urge associated with alcohol.","paragraphIndex":20028},{"label":"Clinical principle","explanation":"Treatment choice depends on the person's medical situation and goals; this textbook explains biological mechanisms, not an instruction to self-medicate.","paragraphIndex":20029},{"label":"Different targets","explanation":"Some medications discourage drinking through physiological reactions; others influence systems involved in reinforcement or craving.","paragraphIndex":78118},{"label":"Clinical significance","explanation":"Evidence and suitability vary. A medication is not interchangeable with psychological support, and the existence of a drug does not mean every person's problem has the same biological cause.","paragraphIndex":78119}],"status":"original_classroom_note_sample","basis":"provided_book_pdf_and_markdown","followUpExplanation":"Medication approaches for alcohol-use problems target different aspects of drinking behavior, such as unpleasant effects after alcohol or the rewarding consequences of drinking.","followUpParagraphIndex":45409,"depth":"comprehensive_masters_with_expanded_explanations"},{"headingId":"bp14-m14-1-h11","title":"Medications to Combat Opiate Abuse","level":2,"parentId":"bp14-m14-1-h09","printedPage":467,"pdfPage":485,"explanation":"Opiates act at opioid receptors, so one treatment strategy is to occupy or block those receptors in a controlled way. This can reduce unstable cycles of intoxication and withdrawal.","paragraphIndex":20030,"bullets":[{"label":"Agonist approaches","explanation":"A medically managed, longer-acting substitute can stabilize receptor activity and reduce withdrawal and unsafe behavior.","paragraphIndex":20031},{"label":"Antagonist approaches","explanation":"Blocking opioid effects can decrease reinforcement for some patients. Selection and timing require professional assessment because effects and withdrawal risks differ.","paragraphIndex":20032},{"label":"Agonist and antagonist logic","explanation":"Longer-acting receptor stimulation can reduce cycles of intoxication and withdrawal; receptor blockade can prevent some effects of subsequently used opioids.","paragraphIndex":78120},{"label":"Why supervision matters","explanation":"These approaches differ in their requirements, limitations, and risks. The chapter's discussion is explanatory rather than instructions for choosing or using a medication.","paragraphIndex":78121}],"status":"original_classroom_note_sample","basis":"provided_book_pdf_and_markdown","followUpExplanation":"Medications for opioid-use problems can act on opioid receptors to reduce withdrawal, limit intoxication, or block the effects of opioids. Drug effects change neural circuits while those circuits encode habits, expectations and cues that influence later drug use.","paragraphIndex":20033,"bullets":[{"label":"Integrative model","explanation":"Receptor action, reward learning, stress and social circumstances should be examined together, not as competing complete explanations.","paragraphIndex":20034},{"label":"Revision question","explanation":"For any drug, distinguish immediate physiological effects, longer-term adaptation, learned triggers and available treatments.","paragraphIndex":20035},{"label":"Integrate mechanisms","explanation":"Acute drug actions create learning opportunities; repeated use changes neural and behavioral responses; cues and stress can sustain motivation.","paragraphIndex":78122},{"label":"Clinical perspective","explanation":"Effective explanations avoid both moral blame and the assumption that biological risk makes behavior unchangeable.
